scope_findings.claim: The project builds one multisensory biodiversity data-integration system carrying measurement from molecules to satellites, harmonising omics, in-situ and remote-sensing data for enhanced ecosystem-condition assessment.
Three omics layers enter the observation chain: stress metabolomics from P01, and genomic, transcriptomic and environmental-DNA sequencing from P09.
The observation chain runs from in-situ plots through field spectroscopy and uncrewed aerial survey to Copernicus satellite data.
Three demonstration cases sit on one agricultural pressure gradient: farmland and grassland, the freshwater ecotones receiving their runoff, and the coastal transitional waters downstream.
Demonstration cases target habitats and ecotones marked as under pressure or as restoration priorities, selected on evidence of socio-economic pressures rather than data convenience.
The multi-season field archive is reworked into documented training and validation sets with a declared, leakage-safe split protocol.
Deep-learning models scale habitat and ecosystem classification from the three cases to European coverage and predict biodiversity trends.
Every published habitat label carries a crosswalk to EUNIS and to the Global Ecosystem Typology.
Harmonisation workflows and processing protocols are published with provenance and linked to the European Open Science Cloud and the European Common Data Spaces.
Biodiversity indicators are carried into farm-management tools through an existing multi-country user network of agricultural holdings, and practitioner ability to act on them is evaluated.
scope_findings.flag_reason: Borderline against SR-04. SR-04 names agriculture only as a domain whose data is linked to observation data; pushing biodiversity indicators into farm-management decision tools is an uptake/exploitation activity that no loaded Tier 2B scope element clearly requires. Whether it falls within SR-04 depends on project framing. Scope element involved: SR-04.

scope_findings.claim: Effort and budget are earmarked for cooperation with GBIF, OBIS and LUCAS, and project occurrence records are published to them.
Commission-steered grassland and agricultural-landscape monitoring data, including LUCAS grassland and EMBAL, is ingested as a reference layer for the terrestrial case.
The pressures driving each case are analysed as socio-economic drivers rather than treated as background.
Outputs are aligned to reporting obligations under the Habitats Directive, the Birds Directive, the Marine Strategy Framework Directive and the EU Nature Restoration Regulation.
The project contributes its harmonisation decisions to standards bodies as joint definitions of data collection, metadata and processing protocols.
A knowledge-gap and data-need analysis runs before the integration design and prioritises which critical biodiversity knowledge gaps the cases address.
Predictive modelling is delivered at case-site, regional and European scales.
The project delivers FAIR data, harmonisation workflows and processing protocols as named outputs and verifies them on the three cases.
The interoperability work package holds an open place for the Joint Research Centre as a zero-funding beneficiary or associated partner, counted towards no eligibility condition.
The project provides a standing coordination interface to the ESA FuturEO earth-observation projects in the same cluster.
Where a European research infrastructure offers a service the observation chain needs, the project uses it rather than rebuilding it.
The project uses Copernicus and European satellite navigation programmes wherever it uses satellite data.
